Satellite navigation systems (commonly called GNSS, Global Navigation Satellite Systems) operate on the principle of trilateration using precisely timed signals from orbital platforms. Four (4) operational constellations exist: (1) GPS (United States, 31 satellites, MEO at approx. 20,200 km altitude), (2) GLONASS (Russia, 24 satellites), (3) Galileo (EU, 30 satellites planned), and (4) BeiDou (China, 35 satellites including GEO and IGSO orbits). Position accuracy depends on several factors: satellite geometry (quantified by DOP, dilution of precision), atmospheric delays (ionospheric and tropospheric), multipath interference, and receiver clock error. Standard positioning service (SPS) achieves 3-5 m horizontal accuracy (95% confidence). Differential correction techniques (DGPS, RTK) improve accuracy to sub-meter or centimeter levels respectively. RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) requires a base station within approximately 30 km and achieves 1-2 cm accuracy (sufficient for surveying and precision agriculture applications). Dual-frequency receivers (L1/L2 for GPS) enable ionospheric delay estimation and correction.
